claims.text: Increasing aluminum content in a high-entropy-alloy protective coating promotes formation of a continuous, coherent, alumina-rich tribolayer during sliding.
A continuous alumina-rich tribolayer governs and reduces coating wear by limiting adhesive and abrasive damage.
The baseline coating has a balanced equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition.
Conventional deposition produces a relatively uniform baseline microstructure with only moderate oxide formation during wear.
The modified coating contains 10–20% more aluminum than the baseline, with the other elemental proportions adjusted to retain high configurational entropy.
Aluminum enrichment enhances oxidation behavior at the contact surface.
Under the proposed room-temperature ambient sliding conditions, tribochemical reactions are significant without inducing thermally driven phase transformations.
Aluminum enrichment drives in situ formation of a nanostructured, continuous alumina-rich tribolayer adherent to the coating.
During sliding, excess aluminum selectively oxidizes to form Al2O3.
The Al2O3 tribolayer acts as a barrier that reduces direct metal-to-metal and abrasive contact.
Reduced direct and abrasive contact lowers friction and wear rate.
Relative to the baseline, the aluminum-enriched coating will have a significantly lower wear rate and friction coefficient.
The aluminum-enriched coating will show a more continuous and coherent alumina-rich layer on its worn surface.
The baseline coating forms a less coherent or discontinuous tribolayer and consequently has a higher wear rate under identical conditions.
The proposed protective effect holds at moderate contact pressures and sliding speeds in ambient conditions but may be limited at extremely high loads, speeds, or temperatures.
